I still rank **D** first, and I think Colleague 10’s round 3 statement actually strengthens D more than C. He concedes that C is only Rawlsian if “poorer citizens with fewer resources” is read as “those excluded from genuinely fair cooperative terms by systemic inequality.” But that gloss is not in C’s text; it is exactly what D states directly. C says civic obligations bind those in fair systems, “which is not true of poorer citizens with fewer resources.” Read literally, that makes fewer resources sound like the operative exception. If C needs an unstated systemic-injustice qualification to avoid becoming a resource test, then the qualification is doing the real work—and D already names it.

The agency objection can also be met without denying Rawlsian moral agency. Rawls distinguishes the **natural duty of justice**, which may still apply to persons as such, from **obligations under the principle of fairness/reciprocity**, which depend on reasonably just institutions and fair terms of cooperation. D’s phrase “not a product of their own agency” should be read within that second domain: when systemic inequality undermines fair value of political liberties, fair equality of opportunity, labor markets, political influence, wealth transmission, and the social bases of self-respect, failure to fulfill reciprocity-based civic obligations is not properly attributed as ordinary individual moral failure. That does not say poorer citizens lack moral powers; it says reciprocity itself has been compromised by the basic structure.

Nor is this merely downstream blame-talk. The question asks about Rawlsian reciprocity in the context of poverty. Reciprocity is not only an abstract fair-system condition; it concerns whether citizens can reasonably see themselves as participants in fair cooperation. Where poverty is structurally produced, that reciprocal relation is distorted. C states the general condition, but D better captures the poverty-specific point.

So if we are willing to read C charitably beyond its wording, consistency requires reading D charitably too. Read narrowly, D preserves agency and natural duty while explaining why reciprocity-based civic failure under systemic poverty should not be treated as a straightforward product of individual agency. E makes contribution sound unconditional, and A/B remain less plausible. I continue to support **D**.

My disagreement is not with that premise; it is with the idea that **C** is the better statement of the answer for the poverty-specific question.

The key distinction is between the **natural duty of justice**, which Rawls can still hold applies to citizens as moral persons, and **obligations under the principle of fairness/reciprocity**, which depend on reasonably just institutions and fair terms of cooperation. D’s phrase “not a product of their own agency” should be read within that second domain. It need not deny that poorer citizens are moral agents or that they retain a natural duty of justice. It says that when systemic inequality has distorted the background conditions of reciprocity—unequal schools, labor markets, political influence, wealth transmission, and the social bases of self-respect—failure to fulfill reciprocity-based civic obligations is not properly treated as a straightforward individual moral failure. That is an attribution claim internal to reciprocity, not a metaphysical denial of agency.

That is also why the “D is downstream” objection is weaker than it first appears. In the context of poverty, the fairness of attribution is not a separate afterthought. Reciprocity just is the fair terms of cooperation between citizens. If those terms are systematically undermined, then the reciprocal relation itself is compromised, and nonfulfillment cannot be assigned in the ordinary moralized way. D names this poverty-specific distortion directly.

By contrast, C’s wording is doing something less precise. It says civic obligations bind those in fair systems, “which is not true of poorer citizens with fewer resources.” Read literally, that makes having fewer resources the operative exception. Almost every defense of C now adds the qualification: “not fewer resources as such, but systemic exclusion from fair cooperation.” I agree with that qualification. But if that qualification is necessary to make C Rawlsian, then the qualification is doing most of the work—and D already states it.

Read that way, C states the general conditional premise, while D explains why that premise matters specifically for citizens experiencing poverty. The question asks about Rawlsian reciprocity in the context of poverty, not about the abstract fair-system condition alone. D captures the systemic inequality that actually undermines reciprocity and explains why nonfulfillment is not straightforwardly attributable to individual agency under those conditions.

E may preserve a general moral duty, but the question is about reciprocity, and E makes contribution sound unconditional. A is too dismissive, and B is unnecessary. If we take the C camp’s own structural reading seriously, D remains the more precise and poverty-specific interpretation of Rawlsian reciprocity.

The decisive issue for me is that the question asks about Rawls’s concept of **reciprocity itself**, not about the downstream attribution of blame or failure. Rawlsian reciprocity belongs to society as a fair system of cooperation: civic obligations under the principle of fairness bind when institutions are reasonably just and citizens can reasonably regard themselves as receiving fair benefits and bearing fair burdens. In the context of poverty, systemic inequality matters because it can undermine the background conditions of reciprocity—fair equality of opportunity, the fair value of political liberties, the difference principle, and the social bases of self-respect. That is what C captures: reciprocity-based civic obligations are conditional on a fair system, and poorer citizens may not genuinely be included in such a system.

I agree that **D** names an important poverty-specific consequence: where systemic injustice distorts the terms of cooperation, failure to fulfill civic obligations should not be crudely moralized as simple individual failure. But D as written says this failure is “not a product of their own agency,” and that is too strong for Rawls. Rawls preserves moral agency and the natural duty of justice even under unjust institutions. If D is softened to mean “not fairly attributable in the ordinary way,” then it becomes a corollary of C rather than a better interpretation of reciprocity. If it is not softened, it risks contradicting Rawls’s conception of citizens as responsible moral agents.

So my current position is: **C is the most reasonable answer**, read as saying that reciprocity-based civic obligations presuppose fair terms of social cooperation, and systemic poverty can exclude citizens from those fair terms. It should not be read as the crude claim that having fewer resources by itself cancels moral duty or agency. D may state the poverty-context consequence more dramatically, but C states the core Rawlsian concept more directly. E conflates the natural duty of justice with reciprocity, while A and B remain unsupported.
